# Week 6, Day 4.1 - Prerequisites check

**No new TypeScript today.** Jenkins runs commands; it does not care what language wrote them.

| In play | Taught in |
|---|---|
| `Deno.Command`, exit codes | [day3_1](/learn/w6/d3/p1) |
| Objects as config | [week3/day1_1](/learn/w3/d1/p1) |
| `package.json` scripts | [week5/day1_3](/learn/w5/d1/p3) |

The one idea worth five minutes is not syntax - it is that **`package.json` is an interface**.

**Next:** [Day 4.2 - Jenkins](/learn/w6/d4/p2)

## `package.json` scripts as the contract

A `scripts` entry gives a long command a short name:

```json
"scripts": {
  "test:smoke": "playwright test -c week5/generated/day1-smoke.config.ts"
}
```

`npm run test:smoke` now runs it. The reason this matters for CI:

| CI knows | CI does not need to know |
|---|---|
| `npm run test:smoke` | which config, which folder, which grep, which browser |

Change the config and CI keeps working. Encode the config **in** the CI job and every change is
a change in two places - one of which needs a Jenkins login.

The last three were added for this week. `test:smoke` and `test:regression` point at the two
configs from [week5/day1_2](/learn/w5/d1/p2) - so the suites you built there are now
callable by name, which is exactly what a CI job needs.

# Week 6, Day 4.2 - Jenkins

So far every test run has started with you typing a command. That does not survive contact with a
team: someone is on holiday, someone deploys at 11pm, someone forgets.

Jenkins is a server that runs your command instead.

> **Mode: read-and-do.** Jenkins is a web UI, so unlike everything else in this course **these
> steps are not executed by a cell.** The *commands* Jenkins runs are - at the bottom of this
> lesson.

## Where it fits

| Tool | Job |
|---|---|
| **GitHub** | stores the code - [day3_2](/learn/w6/d3/p2) |
| **Jenkins** | fetches it and runs it |

And the term: **CI/CD** - continuous integration, continuous deployment. Developers integrate and
deploy; your tests are what makes that safe. Which is why a tester ends up in the Jenkins UI.

## Setup, once

| Step | Detail |
|---|---|
| Install | `jenkins.io/download` - the Windows installer is fine |
| Needs **Java** | Jenkins runs on the JVM. Java **17 or 21** (LTS) |
| Opens at | `http://localhost:8080` |
| First screen asks for | an admin password, in a file whose path it prints |
| Then | "Install suggested plugins", and create your own username |

> Java version bites people. Check with `java -version`. A very new JDK is **not** safer here -
> Jenkins supports specific LTS releases, and this machine's Java 26 is outside that list.

Check the Java line against Jenkins' supported releases (**17** or **21**) before you install.
A newer JDK is not safer here - it is simply untested, and this machine reports one that is
outside the supported list.

## Job 1 - run the tests already on this machine

**New Item → name it `playwright_local_test` → Freestyle project → OK.**

| Section | What to set |
|---|---|
| Source Code Management | **None** - the code is already here |
| General → Advanced → **Use custom workspace** | the folder holding your `package.json` |
| Build Steps → Add → **Execute Windows batch command** | `npm run test:smoke` |

Then **Build Now**, and open **Console Output** to watch it.

The custom workspace is the part that confuses everyone: without it Jenkins runs in **its own**
empty folder, finds no `package.json`, and the command fails for a reason that looks nothing like
the real one.

## The first build fails. Twice.

Both failures are expected on a fresh agent, and both are one-time fixes.

| Console says | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `'playwright' is not recognized...` | no packages installed | add `npm ci` above your command |
| `Executable doesn't exist at ...` / browser missing | no browser binaries | add `npx playwright install --with-deps` |

Run each once, then **delete it from the build step** - they are setup, not part of every run.

| Command | Why not `npm install` |
|---|---|
| `npm ci` | installs the **exact** locked versions and fails if the lockfile disagrees. Repeatable, which is the whole point of CI |

## Job 2 - one script instead of the suite

Same job, different batch command - anything you can type locally:

```
npx playwright test week6/generated/day1-pom-structure.spec.ts
```

## Job 3 - fetch the code from GitHub

This is the one that matters, because it stops depending on your laptop.

| Section | What to set |
|---|---|
| Source Code Management | **Git** |
| Repository URL | your repo's HTTPS clone URL |
| Credentials | none for a public repo; required for a private one |
| Branches to build | `*/master` - **or `*/main`.** See [day3_2](/learn/w6/d3/p2) |
| Build Steps | `npm run test:smoke`, as before |

No custom workspace now: Jenkins clones into a workspace it owns. That is the difference between
the two jobs - *where the code comes from*, nothing else.

## The part that IS verifiable

Everything above is clicking. The batch command is where builds actually fail, so run the
sequence here.

| Line | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `npm ci` skipped | it deletes `node_modules` and rebuilds; right on a CI agent, wrong in your working copy |
| `playwright --version` answers | the CLI resolves - what the first Jenkins failure was really about |
| smoke suite `exit 0` | **green build.** Non-zero is red. That is the entire contract |

## A faster loop than either

Before reaching for CI to run one test: the **Playwright VS Code extension** puts a green arrow
in the gutter next to every `test()` and `describe()`. Click it and that test runs.

| Want to run | Use |
|---|---|
| One test, while writing it | the gutter arrow |
| The suite, before pushing | `npm run test:smoke` |
| The suite, on every push, without being asked | Jenkins - or [day5_2](/learn/w6/d5/p2) |

## Common mistakes

| Mistake | Symptom |
|---|---|
| No custom workspace on a local job | `package.json` not found |
| `npm ci` left in the build step forever | every build reinstalls; minutes wasted |
| `headless: false` in the config | CI has no display; the run hangs or crashes |
| `*/master` when the branch is `main` | Jenkins clones, finds nothing to build |
| Encoding the config in the Jenkins job | the next config change needs a Jenkins login |

**Next:** [Day 4.3 - Naming your suites](/learn/w6/d4/p3)

# Week 6, Day 4.3 - Naming your suites

Same `npm run`, arranged so the CI job never changes again.

## The payoff from week 5

[Week 5 Day 1](/learn/w5/d1/p2) built two configs over one spec and asked you to trust that
it mattered. This is why:

```json
"test:smoke":      "playwright test -c week5/generated/day1-smoke.config.ts",
"test:regression": "playwright test -c week5/generated/day1-regression.config.ts"
```

| Jenkins job | Batch command | Runs |
|---|---|---|
| `playwright_smoke` | `npm run test:smoke` | **2** tests |
| `playwright_regression` | `npm run test:regression` | **4** tests |

Two jobs, two one-word commands, and neither knows what a config is.

Two versus four, selected by a name. A CI job that says `npm run test:smoke` keeps working when
you change the tag, the browser, or the worker count.

## The naming a team actually uses

| Script | Runs when | Budget |
|---|---|---|
| `test:smoke` | every push | ~2 minutes |
| `test:sanity` | after a deploy | ~10 minutes |
| `test:regression` | nightly | as long as it takes |

The session's advice, and it holds: name them after **when they run**, not after what they touch.
"When do I run this?" is the question a CI job is answering.

## Jenkins on your laptop is not CI

The session is candid about this, and it is worth being blunt:

| | Jenkins on your machine | A hosted runner |
|---|---|---|
| Who can reach it | you | the team |
| Runs when your laptop is shut | no | yes |
| Parallel machines | one | as many as you pay for |
| Who patches it | **you** | them |

A local Jenkins is a **rehearsal**. It teaches the model - job, workspace, build step, console
output, exit code - and that model transfers unchanged to [day5_2](/learn/w6/d5/p2).

## Headless, always

Jenkins has no screen. `headless: false` committed to a config is the classic way to make a suite
that passes locally and hangs in CI - see [week3/day5_2](/learn/w3/d5/p2).

**Next:** [Day 4.4 - Practice](/learn/w6/d4/p4)

# Week 6, Day 4.4 - Practice

Problems 1-5 need Jenkins installed. If you have not got it yet, 6 and 7 do not.
**Next:** [Day 5.1 - Prerequisites](/learn/w6/d5/p1)

problems.statement:
**Get to a green build**
Install Jenkins, create `playwright_local_test`, point it at this folder, run `npm run test:smoke`.

**Right when:** Console Output ends with `2 passed` and the build is blue/green - and you hit both
first-build failures on the way and can say what each meant.

**Break the workspace on purpose**
Clear the custom workspace and build again.

**Right when:** you can quote the error and explain it in terms of *which folder* Jenkins was in.

**Two jobs, one repo**
Create `playwright_smoke` and `playwright_regression` as separate jobs.

**Right when:** they report **2** and **4** tests, and neither job mentions a config file.

**Build from GitHub**
Push your work ([day3_2](/learn/w6/d3/p2)), then make a job with SCM = Git against your own URL.

**Right when:** it passes with **no** custom workspace set - and you can say where the code came
from and which branch name you used.

**Make it red**
Change one assertion so it fails, push, and rebuild.

**Right when:** the build goes red, and you can point at the exit code as the reason - not at the
test name.

**A suite of your own**
Add `test:week6` variants to `package.json`: one for Day 1's spec, one for Day 2's.

**Right when:** each runs the count you predicted, and you wrote the prediction down first.

**Find the headless trap**
Set `headless: false` in a copy of a config, then run it through `day4-ci-commands.ts`.

**Right when:** you can describe what a CI agent with no display would do with that run, and say
which file should never carry that setting.
